newsitem.title: USA: U.S. copper premiums to soften as arbitrage shifts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. copper premiums to soften as arbitrage shifts.

text.p: Spot copper merchant premiums are softening in the U.S. as the arbitrage shifts to a COMEX premium over LME, making LME warrants cheaper in the Midwest and encouraging imports of South American metal, dealers said.

Premiums currently range between 2.50 and 2.75 cents in the Midwest, down from a solid 2.75 cents last week. In the Northeast, premiums are 2.75 to 3.00 cents, down from a high of 4.00 to 5.00 cents in June.
Last week, the LME cash price was trading as much as 6.50 cents over COMEX, which led many merchants and producers to park their metal in LME warehouses to exploit the arbitrage.
But at 0815 EDT Wednesday, the COMEX spot price was trading at a 2.55-cent premium to the LME cash price as London traders hammered the LME spreads in the last week.
Consequently, holders of LME warrants in St. Louis and other locations will are cutting their premiums to find U.S. customers, who price copper based on the Comex price.
"Premiums have softened since the arbitrage shifted," a New York physical dealer said. "It doesn't pay to keep metal in St. Louis if you can find a customer."
Asked if he was finding customers, he replied, "The rod mills are still busy."
A Midwest merchant pointed out that the arbitrage shift would probably attract off-grade metal imports from South America.

"There's a lot of off-grade and electrowon metal coming into the U.S. from South America," one merchant said. "Business in Asia has been in the pits. So they've been taking a gamble by sending their copper to U.S. hoping that the arbitrage will shift."
In the Northeast, premiums are expected to decline as Inco Ltd restarts its 102,500-tonne Sudbury mine in Ontario next month. The mine is closed for July for its annual maintanence shutdown.
In June, the mine was felled by a month-long strike. At that point, premiums reached as high as 4.00-5.00 cents. "By next month, they should be back to 2.75 cents," one merchant said.
((Derek J. Caney, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1640))
